## Summary

Lithium-ion remains the core EV traction-battery platform. The current market is primarily split between lower-cost LFP/phosphate systems and higher-energy NMC/NCA/NMCA systems. Future EV-relevant technologies include manganese-rich lithium-ion, sodium-ion, silicon-enhanced anodes, semi-solid or quasi-solid cells, all-solid-state lithium-metal, lithium-metal/anode-free designs, and lithium-sulfur.

## Current Commercial Baseline

LFP and NMC-family lithium-ion batteries are the validated mainstream chemistries. IEA reports LFP was nearly half of global EV battery sales in 2024, with China as the strongest production and adoption center. NMC and related high-nickel chemistries remain more common in the United States and Europe.

LFP's main strengths are low cost, long cycle life, no nickel or cobalt, thermal stability, and stronger tolerance for routine 100% charging. Its weaknesses are lower gravimetric and volumetric energy density and weaker cold-weather performance.

NMC, NCA, and NMCA retain advantages for long-range, high-performance, cold-climate, and packaging-constrained EVs. Their weaknesses are cost, nickel and cobalt exposure, higher supply-chain and emissions risk, and greater sensitivity to charge-management practices.

## Bridge Chemistries

LMFP/LFMP and other phosphate variants aim to raise LFP energy density while preserving low cost and cobalt-free advantages.

LMR and other high-manganese lithium-ion cathodes aim to bridge the gap between LFP cost and high-nickel energy density. GM and LG Energy Solution plan LMR prismatic cell commercialization for GM trucks and full-size SUVs, with pre-production expected in late 2027 and commercial production planned in the United States by 2028.

Silicon-enhanced lithium-ion is an anode-side improvement rather than a full chemistry replacement. It is likely to arrive through incremental increases in silicon content before any broad shift to silicon-dominant anodes.

## Emerging Chemistries

Sodium-ion is credible for short-range, low-cost, cold-climate, and dual-chemistry use cases, but lower energy density limits its use in long-range passenger cars.

Semi-solid and quasi-solid cells are likely to be the first consumer-facing "solid-state" products because they reduce liquid electrolyte without requiring full all-solid-state manufacturing maturity.

All-solid-state lithium-metal batteries are promising but not yet mass-market. Toyota targets 2027-2028 launch timing, BMW is testing Solid Power cells, and QuantumScape shipped B1 QSE-5 samples in 2025. IEA characterizes solid-state as large pilot stage with limited initial volumes.

Lithium-sulfur has high theoretical energy and lower critical-mineral exposure, but cycle life, volumetric density, lithium-metal stability, and automotive qualification remain unresolved.

## Boundary Technologies

NiMH remains relevant for hybrids, lead-acid for low-voltage auxiliary systems, LTO for extreme-cycle and fast-charge specialty use, and LMO for historical or blended contexts. Metal-air, redox-flow, and iron-air are more relevant to grid or specialty systems than mainstream passenger BEV traction.

## Key Caveats

"Solid-state" is used inconsistently across industry sources. It may refer to all-solid, semi-solid, quasi-solid, gel, or hybrid electrolyte systems.

Commercialization claims are not equivalent to mass-market impact. A concept vehicle, demo fleet, sample shipment, pilot line, and high-volume vehicle program imply very different levels of readiness.

Battery chemistry is only one part of EV value. Pack size, charging curve, thermal management, warranty, replacement cost, charging standard, software support, and brand service network also affect residual value.
